title.narrative: Saint Lucia Health System Strengthening Project

description.narrative: The development objective is to improve the accessibility, efficiency, and responsiveness of key health services, and provide a response in the event of eligible crises or emergencies.

The development objective of the Health System Strengthening Project for Saint Lucia is to improve the accessibility, efficiency, and responsiveness of key health services. The project comprises of four components. The first component, design and implementation of an essential benefits package focuses on the demand side and includes the review of the design and implementation of the benefits package, including administration, purchasing and contracting arrangements, regulations surrounding the scheme, and potential sources of additional revenue for expanding health service coverage. It consists of following sub-components: (i) review of the essential benefits package; and (ii) implementation of the essential benefits package. The second component, strengthening service delivery in support of the essential benefits package consists of following sub-components: (i) improving service delivery through performance-based financing (PBF); (ii) strengthening the supply of health care services; and (iii) public health emergency preparedness and response. The third component, institutional capacity building, project management, and coordination will cover project implementation efforts, including project management, fiduciary tasks, and monitoring and evaluation (M and E) associated with supervision of the project. The fourth component, contingent emergency response component (CERC) will provide funding following an eligible emergency. It will include conditions for the use of funds, and will only be triggered when certain actions, as agreed by the government and the Bank are met.

title.narrative: Percentage of persons in the ATP living with Diabetes who are managed by the PBF facilities, according to OM protocols

comment.narrative: Reduction of Target from 20 percent to 10 percent. Contributing factors are: (1) values of blood pressure, weight, height, BMI and prescriptions (attributes) not consistently recorded, (2) non-adherence to care by persons living with Diabetes and Hypertension, (3) unavailability of free HB1AC test for Diabetes Screening, and (4) high-risk patients not accessing care. Given the complex requirement to satisfy these indicators, the current 20 percent target is very ambitious; following a technical review, 10 percent is established as a reasonable target. Efforts to further advance from a zero baseline include hiring of data entry clerks to update records, sensitization of clinical staff to increase data entry efforts, aggressive engagement to conduct community campaigns to mobilize persons into care, and procurement of portable HB1AC machines for Diabetes screening.

title.narrative: Number of diabetes and hypertension outreach campaigns successfully conducted by public primary health facilities

comment.narrative: Outreach campaigns to scale-up screening for Diabetes and hypertension commenced in September 2023. As of October 30th 2024 a total of 51 outreach activities has taken place. The total is cumulative. As of August 2024 this indicator has achieved its target. We continues to reiterate that objectives of each outreach needs to be stated and used as a guide to determine the success of any outreach. Assessment of results of each outreach will enable the identification of best practices that can be adopted. Statistics on outreach activities are captured in SLUHIS and all activities are closely monitored to ensure timely data entry into SLUHIS. A total of 1382 clients were seen during the 51 outreach activities of which 701 were from the ATP. 11 of the 17 Wellness Centers conducted outreach activities as of October 2024.

title.narrative: Percentage of persons in the ATP living with Hypertension who are managed by the PBF facilities, according to OM protocols

comment.narrative: The original target for this indicator was set without availability of baseline data as this indicator requires recording performance on quality of care. In the absence of observational baseline data, this target was overestimated. The PBFâ€™s operational evaluation during Phase 1 of the PBF Pilot has provided observational data to inform the recalibration of these targets. It has also guided the PIU / PBF team on actions to improve this treatment related indicator through the following: (1) continuous training on data entry and scaling up BCC, sensitization); (2) proactive tracking of follow-up appointments (3) retroactive entry of the quality attributes for patient visits based on paper-based records; (4) review and revise data entry authority; and (5) leverage the financial incentives to boost data entry. The finding of the low baseline values reinforces the importance of including incentives for quality of care.
